power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Random-effect predictions from multilevel models are often used to relate individual differences in processes, such as growth or stress reactivity, to other variables.
Yet, regressions using these predictions can distort regression coefficients and standard errors because the predictions combine shrinkage with sampling error.
Here, we introduce and evaluate Random-Effect Prediction Adjustment for Inference in Regression (REPAIR), a two-step framework for linear regressions involving random effects.
For linear Gaussian multilevel models, REPAIR obtains likelihood-only predictions by generalized least squares.
A regularized method-of-moments estimator then uses estimated cluster-specific sampling-error covariances to correct structural moments.
Four simulation studies examined random effects as predictors, outcomes, or both, including unequal cluster sizes.
REPAIR generally showed small bias at medium to high predictor reliability and often had lower root mean squared error than alternative methods.
Low predictor reliability remained challenging, particularly for confidence interval coverage in small samples.
These findings support REPAIR as a practical framework for estimating structural relationships involving random effects while accounting for their measurement uncertainty.
Many psychological studies concern individual differences in processes that unfold over time or across situations (Hamaker & Wichers, 2017).
text.formatted: Many psychological studies concern individual differences in processes that unfold over time or across situations <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Hamaker & Wichers, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Researchers may ask whether people who improve more rapidly during treatment experience better subsequent outcomes, whether long-term personality or behavior change predicts life outcomes, or how cognitive processes elicited by an experimental task relate to mental health.

Multilevel models (MLMs) are natural tools for such questions because they distinguish population-average effects from person-specific deviations representing individual levels or within-person associations (Raudenbush & Bryk, 2010).
text.formatted: Multilevel models (MLMs) are natural tools for such questions because they distinguish population-average effects from person-specific deviations representing individual levels or within-person associations <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Raudenbush & Bryk, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: A common analytic strategy is to fit an MLM, extract its random-effects predictions, and use those predictions in a second analysis (Liu & Rhemtulla, 2022).
text.formatted: A common analytic strategy is to fit an MLM, extract its random-effects predictions, and use those predictions in a second analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Liu & Rhemtulla, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The scientific goal, however, is typically to understand relationships among the underlying person-specific processes, rather than merely among their model-predicted values.
This distinction matters in a range of applications.

For example, in a randomized meditation trial, Webb et al. (2024) predicted person-specific rates of change in mindfulness, then examined whether these mediated the overall effect of the intervention on subsequent distress.
text.formatted: For example, in a randomized meditation trial, <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Webb et al. (2024)</ref> predicted person-specific rates of change in mindfulness, then examined whether these mediated the overall effect of the intervention on subsequent distress.

text.text: Other researchers have considered whether random intercepts and slopes from MLMs capture meaningful psychological attributes.

For example, drawing on five ecological momentary assessment (EMA) studies, Kuper and colleagues 2022 predicted within-person relationships between Big Five personality states and eight situation-specific characteristics (e.g., whether the situation was experienced as pleasant).

To better understand personality-situation contingencies, they then examined the reliability, short-term stability, external correlates, and latent structure of the 40 random slopes extracted from the MLMs.

In both of these examples, as well as numerous others (e.g., Hallquist and Lenzenweger, 2013; McCormick et al., 2026; Willroth et al., 2025), the substantive goal is to characterize individual differences in within-person processes, such as change or decision-making.
text.formatted: In both of these examples, as well as numerous others (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Hallquist and Lenzenweger, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">McCormick et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Willroth et al., 2025)</ref>, the substantive goal is to characterize individual differences in within-person processes, such as change or decision-making.

text.text: The shared statistical strategy is to predict person-specific values of those processes from repeated observations and then use them as variables in a downstream analysis.
A standard approach for predicting person-specific random effects is Empirical Bayes (EB) (Robinson, 1991).
text.formatted: A standard approach for predicting person-specific random effects is Empirical Bayes (EB) <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Robinson, 1991)</ref>.

text.text: EB predictions borrow information from the full sample, shrinking uncertain individual values toward the population mean.
This adaptive shrinkage can substantially improve the predictions of individual values (Katahira, 2016).
text.formatted: This adaptive shrinkage can substantially improve the predictions of individual values <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Katahira, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: When the goal is to estimate relationships among underlying random effects, however, shrinkage complicates the use of EB predictions as observed variables (Liu & Rhemtulla, 2022; Liu et al., 2021).
text.formatted: When the goal is to estimate relationships among underlying random effects, however, shrinkage complicates the use of EB predictions as observed variables <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Liu & Rhemtulla, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Liu et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Shrinkage changes the variances and covariances of EB predictions, so downstream analyses using these as outcomes or predictors may not recover the true relationships involving the underlying random effects.
The predictions also retain sampling error; treating them as perfectly measured can distort structural estimates and their standard errors (Bollen, 1989; Cohen et al., 2015; Fuller, 1987).
text.formatted: The predictions also retain sampling error; treating them as perfectly measured can distort structural estimates and their standard errors <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bollen, 1989;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Cohen et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Fuller, 1987)</ref>.

text.text: Here, we develop a two-step framework-Random-Effect Prediction Adjustment for Inference in Regression (REPAIR)-that accounts for shrinkage and uncertainty in random-effect predictions.
The first step produces likelihoodonly predictions and their cluster/person-specific sampling error covariances within an MLM framework.
The second step uses those covariances in a modified method-of-moments errors-in-variables regression that extends established measurement error models (Fuller, 1987).
text.formatted: The second step uses those covariances in a modified method-of-moments errors-in-variables regression that extends established measurement error models <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Fuller, 1987)</ref>.

text.text: This framework offers a practical way to investigate relationships among person-specific processes measured across different tasks, settings, or timescales.

Although our examples emphasize within-person processes arising from repeated observations, we note that the methods presented here apply equally to other forms of clustering such as students nested within classrooms.
>Existing Approaches
text.formatted: <head n="2." >Existing Approaches</head>

text.text: The most direct solution to avoiding the problems of treating EB predictions as ordinary variables is not to rely on random-effect predictions at all.

A joint model can simultaneously specify an MLM linking observed data to underlying random effects and a structural model describing how those effects relate to one another or to other variables, accounting for uncertainty in the random effects through the full likelihood.

Joint modeling might involve simply incorporating person-level variables into an MLM through a cross-level interaction, or fitting latent curve models (Bollen & Curran, 2006), multilevel structural equation models, or other joint latent variable models when a random effect predicts a distal outcome or participates in a more complex path model.
text.formatted: Joint modeling might involve simply incorporating person-level variables into an MLM through a cross-level interaction, or fitting latent curve models <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Bollen & Curran, 2006)</ref>, multilevel structural equation models, or other joint latent variable models when a random effect predicts a distal outcome or participates in a more complex path model.

text.text: Joint modeling is not always practical, however.
Researchers often collect repeated measures from several tasks or assessments within the same study, yet these observations may not have a natural occasion-level correspondence.

This can lead to difficulties in specification and estimation when model complexity grows (Hickey et al., 2016; Rustand et al., 2024), or loss of information about uncertainty when "shortcuts" such as taking averages or percentages are used (Haines et al., 2025).
text.formatted: This can lead to difficulties in specification and estimation when model complexity grows <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Hickey et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Rustand et al., 2024)</ref>, or loss of information about uncertainty when "shortcuts" such as taking averages or percentages are used <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Haines et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Two-step approaches offer a practical alternative by representing each latent process or trait with a separately fitted MLM.

Information from these models is then carried into a second-step structural analysis estimating relationships among the processes or traits while accounting for measurement error (Lai & Liu, 2026; Rosseel & Loh, 2024).
text.formatted: Information from these models is then carried into a second-step structural analysis estimating relationships among the processes or traits while accounting for measurement error <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Lai & Liu, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Rosseel & Loh, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: A separate motivation for two-step estimation is to hold a vetted step 1 model fixed while comparing structural models.

Estimating the step 1 model separately can prevent misspecification in the structural model from biasing step 1 model parameter estimates, a phenomenon known as interpretational confounding (Bollen et al., 2007; Burt, 1973 Burt, , 1976)).
text.formatted: Estimating the step 1 model separately can prevent misspecification in the structural model from biasing step 1 model parameter estimates, a phenomenon known as interpretational confounding <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Bollen et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Burt, 1973</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Burt, , 1976))</ref>.

text.text: Similar motivations underlie structural-after-measurement and other multi-step latent-variable procedures (Bollen, 1996; Kuha & Bakk, 2024; Levy, 2023; Rosseel & Loh, 2024).
text.formatted: Similar motivations underlie structural-after-measurement and other multi-step latent-variable procedures <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bollen, 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Kuha & Bakk, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Levy, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Rosseel & Loh, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: These advantages depend on an appropriately specified first-step model and a second-step procedure that accounts for how the latent quantities were measured.

Modularized estimation procedures in structural equation modeling (SEM) address how to estimate relationships among latent traits while accounting for measurement error using models that map those traits to observed indicators.

Examples of modularized estimation frameworks include factor score regression (Skrondal & Laake, 2001), the structural-aftermeasurement approach (Rosseel & Loh, 2024), measurement and uncertainty preserving parametric modeling (Levy, 2023), and model-implied instrumental variable, two-stage least squares estimation (Bollen, 1996).
text.formatted: Examples of modularized estimation frameworks include factor score regression <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Skrondal & Laake, 2001)</ref>, the structural-aftermeasurement approach <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Rosseel & Loh, 2024)</ref>, measurement and uncertainty preserving parametric modeling <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Levy, 2023)</ref>, and model-implied instrumental variable, two-stage least squares estimation <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bollen, 1996)</ref>.

text.text: Factor score regression provides a particularly direct parallel to downstream analyses of random-effect predictions.
Factor scores predict individuals' values on latent factors, much as random-effect predictions do for person-specific intercepts or slopes.
This connection also has a formal basis: random effects are latent variables, and MLMs can be represented as SEMs (Bauer, 2003; Curran, 2003).
text.formatted: This connection also has a formal basis: random effects are latent variables, and MLMs can be represented as SEMs <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bauer, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Curran, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Using either type of prediction in a subsequent regression raises the same essential question: how do the prediction method and its corresponding error affect estimates of structural relationships among the latent variables?
Skrondal and Laake (2001) showed that the appropriate factor scoring method can depend on the score's role in the structural model.
text.formatted: <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Skrondal and Laake (2001)</ref> showed that the appropriate factor scoring method can depend on the score's role in the structural model.

text.text: Under their model assumptions, pairing regression-method scores for predictors with Bartlett scores for outcomes yields consistent estimates of unstandardized regression coefficients.
Regression-method scores are analogous to EB predictions, whereas Bartlett scores are analogous to likelihood-only predictions.
This result shows that shrinkage does not necessarily bias a structural regression coefficient.
However, consistency of these coefficients does not imply that the scores' variances and covariances are equal to those of the underlying latent variables (McDonald, 1981; ten Berge et al., 1999).
text.formatted: However, consistency of these coefficients does not imply that the scores' variances and covariances are equal to those of the underlying latent variables <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(McDonald, 1981;</ref> <ref type="bibr">ten Berge et al., 1999)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, standardizing the regression coefficients using the score variance can induce bias (Devlieger et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Consequently, standardizing the regression coefficients using the score variance can induce bias <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Devlieger et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: The measurement error structure can also affect standard errors, so coefficient consistency alone does not establish the validity of conventional inference (Saxonhouse, 1976).
text.formatted: The measurement error structure can also affect standard errors, so coefficient consistency alone does not establish the validity of conventional inference <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Saxonhouse, 1976)</ref>.

text.text: These considerations motivate the complementary approach of correcting score variances and covariances before estimating structural relationships. Croon (2002) developed such a correction that accounts for both the transformation of the latent variables and the error introduced by scoring.
text.formatted: These considerations motivate the complementary approach of correcting score variances and covariances before estimating structural relationships. <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Croon (2002)</ref> developed such a correction that accounts for both the transformation of the latent variables and the error introduced by scoring.

text.text: The central logic follows classical errors-in-variables: for scores already expressed as a latent value plus sampling error, their observed covariance contains separable latent and error components.
Thus, subtracting the expected error covariance recovers the moment matrix relevant to the latent structural relation.
Croon's method additionally generalizes to factor scores without a clean "latent value plus error" structure.

For scoring methods that also transform the latent variables-e.g., via shrinkage, such as regression-method scores-the moment correction must account for both the transformation and the error covariance. Devlieger and Rosseel (2017) found that using Croon's correction in a factor score path analysis achieved higher convergence rates than simultaneous SEM estimation, and Devlieger et al. (2016) introduced an accompanying inferential adjustment.
text.formatted: For scoring methods that also transform the latent variables-e.g., via shrinkage, such as regression-method scores-the moment correction must account for both the transformation and the error covariance. <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Devlieger and Rosseel (2017)</ref> found that using Croon's correction in a factor score path analysis achieved higher convergence rates than simultaneous SEM estimation, and <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Devlieger et al. (2016)</ref> introduced an accompanying inferential adjustment.

text.text: Importantly, however, this approach cannot be applied directly to random-effects predictions because the transformations and error covariances can differ across clusters.
>Role-specific score selection: Skrondal & Laake
text.formatted: <head n="2.2.1." >Role-specific score selection: Skrondal & Laake</head>

text.text: Devlieger and Rosseel (2020) extended Croon's correction to multilevel factor-score regression, estimating structural relationships from corrected within-and between-cluster covariance matrices.
Their between-level correction accounts for sampling variability in cluster means, and their simulations include unequal cluster sizes.
However, their proposed procedure does not accommodate random slopes, which they identify as an important direction for further development.
For these effects, measurement precision depends not only on observation counts but also on cluster-specific predictor designs and residual covariance structures.
In standard linear factor models with common measurement parameters, a given scoring method produces a common score-error covariance across individuals.
Random-effect predictions from MLMs, however, can have cluster-specific error covariances, and thus varying levels of precision.
To address this, Lai and Liu (2026), building on Lai and Hsiao (2022), provide a method for using random-effect predictions from MLMs as predictors and/or outcomes in structural models.
text.formatted: To address this, <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Lai and Liu (2026)</ref>, building on <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Lai and Hsiao (2022)</ref>, provide a method for using random-effect predictions from MLMs as predictors and/or outcomes in structural models.

text.text: They represent each BLUP vector as an indicator of the latent random-effect vector, with person-specific loadings and error covariance carried into a second-step SEM.
This "measurement" model accounts for multivariate shrinkage, correlated errors, and differences in precision across individuals.
Structural parameters are then estimated using an iterative method such as maximum likelihood.
Their approach parallels the "global structural-after-measurement" approach for structural equation models (Rosseel & Loh, 2024).
text.formatted: Their approach parallels the "global structural-after-measurement" approach for structural equation models <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Rosseel & Loh, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: As detailed below, our approach shares this measurement model foundation, but transforms the predictions to an additive-error scale, allowing linear structural regressions to be estimated using corrected moments rather than iterative second-step likelihood estimation.

Numerical stability provides an additional motivation for considering a non-iterative estimator: Lai and Liu (2026) reported limited convergence in some conditions with low intraclass correlations (ICCs) and small cluster sizes, although penalized first-step estimation improved performance.

text.text: This paper makes three contributions.
First, we show that when the shrinkage map is nonsingular, the prior-induced shrinkage in a Gaussian MLM's BLUP can be removed exactly.
The inverse-shrinkage transformation recovers the cluster-specific generalized least-squares, or likelihood-only, prediction.

Crucially, this prediction, as opposed to the BLUP, equals the underlying random effect plus sampling error uncorrelated with that effect, which provides the basis for classical errors-in-variables correction.
Second, we adapt and evaluate the modified method-of-moments (M-MOM) estimator of Fuller (1987) for the second-step structural model involving these predictions.
text.formatted: Second, we adapt and evaluate the modified method-of-moments (M-MOM) estimator of <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Fuller (1987)</ref> for the second-step structural model involving these predictions.

text.text: This estimator accommodates measurement error in predictors and outcomes, including correlated errors and cluster-specific error covariance matrices.

The resulting structural calculations avoid iterative likelihood optimization, although they still require sufficient information, nonsingular corrected matrices, and explicit diagnostics in sparse settings.
Third, we use simulation studies to clarify when the role and precision of random-effect predictions affect structural estimation.
We compare the M-MOM estimator to naive plug-in analyses, simple corrected-moment estimators, Lai and Liu's (2026) two-stage path analysis, and direct joint models when available.
The simulations distinguish random effects used as predictors, outcomes, or both, while varying first-step reliability, random intercept-slope covariance, and cluster-size heterogeneity.
We evaluate bias, precision, inferential performance, and convergence to determine how well each approach recovers relationships among the underlying person-specific processes.
In a Gaussian MLM with known parameters, the conditional mean of a cluster's random effect given its observations is the best linear unbiased predictor (BLUP) (Goldberger, 1962; Henderson, 1973).
text.formatted: In a Gaussian MLM with known parameters, the conditional mean of a cluster's random effect given its observations is the best linear unbiased predictor (BLUP) <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Goldberger, 1962;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Henderson, 1973)</ref>.

text.text: In practice, replacing the population parameters with their fitted values yields EB predictions, also known as empirical BLUPs (EBLUPs).
These predictions balance information from each person's observations with information from the population distribution based on the reliability of a person's observations.
While helpful in some contexts, the shrinkage induced to achieve this balance poses problems for downstream structural analyses.
In regression models, accurate coefficients for target effects depend on their underlying variances and covariances, which may not be preserved in EB predictions.
Classical measurement error models represent an observed value as a sum of its true value and uncorrelated random error (Fuller, 1987).
text.formatted: Classical measurement error models represent an observed value as a sum of its true value and uncorrelated random error <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Fuller, 1987)</ref>.

text.text: Instead, EB predictions contain a shrunken version of the true random effect, so their prediction errors generally covary with the effects being predicted.

Additionally, shrinkage can differ across individuals because of unequal observation counts, different predictor distributions, or different residual covariances, and can be multivariate when a model includes correlated random effects.
These hurdles preclude straightforward strategies for recovering the latent variance, such as subtracting the prediction-error variance from the EB prediction variance.
Instead, our approach first removes this prior-induced shrinkage, then corrects the second-step regression for the remaining sampling error.
The four sections below develop this approach from a scalar intuition to the general multivariate case.
We call our approach Random-Effect Prediction Adjustment for Inference in Regression, or REPAIR.

For EB predictions, this function adaptively assigns weights to the data and to the "prior" population distribution depending on the precision of the data.

Specifically, the EB prediction uses a reliability ratio, or the variance attributable to the random component of the model divided by the total variance found in the (centered) data (Skrondal & Rabe-Hesketh, 2009).

However, likelihood-only predictions can be computed directly.

This is equivalent to the person-specific GLS coefficient vector estimate for the outcome after subtracting the fitted fixed-effect contribution.
When 𝑹 𝑗 = 𝜎 2 𝑰, the error covariance matrix cancels from Equation (4.6), yielding the OLS estimate.

For a random-intercept-random-slope model with the same fixed-and random-effect design matrices, deleting the fitted fixed-effect contribution from Equation (4.6) gives the intercept and slope estimates from a separate OLS regression for each person.
More generally, a diagonal error covariance with unequal entries yields weighted least squares and a nondiagonal error covariance yields GLS.
The benefit of retaining the first-step MLM is therefore distinct from shrinkage of the individual coefficients.
For known MLM parameters, the likelihood-only prediction has conditional sampling-error covariance which follows from Equation (4.5) (see Appendix C).
Under uncorrelated errors with common variance, its plug-in estimate is 𝚿 𝑗 = 𝜎 2 ( 𝒁 ′ 𝑗 𝒁 𝑗 ) -1 .
When the common-variance assumption holds, the MLM pools information across people to estimate 𝜎 2 , potentially improving precision with few or unequal observations per person.
Inverting shrinkage still recovers person-specific OLS slopes, but pooling can stabilize their estimated measurement error covariances, which enter the corrected moments and weights (Appendix D).
This can improve the second-step correction without reducing the sampling variance of the recovered slopes themselves.

Inverting shrinkage restores the classical additive measurement-error form, but Equation (4.5) also shows why unshrinking alone is not a universal second-step correction.

text.text: M-MOM starts with a linear structural equation 𝒃 𝑦 = 𝑩 𝑥 𝜸 + 𝝐, where 𝒃 𝑦 is the true outcome vector, 𝑩 𝑥 is the true predictor matrix, and 𝜸 is the structural coefficient vector of interest.
Predictors and outcomes may include observed variables treated as error-free, as well as random effects.
M-MOM then proceeds in three steps.

First, it obtains a preliminary estimate of 𝜸 by correcting the corresponding moment estimators ( Cov(𝑩 𝑥 , 𝒃 𝑦 ) and ( Var(𝑩 𝑥 )) for measurement error, accounting for both prediction sampling error and correlated errors across predictions.
Second, the regression error variance, Var(𝝐), is estimated using the preliminary estimate of 𝜸 and is similarly corrected for measurement error.
Third, the regression error variance estimate is paired with the measurement error variance estimates to construct cluster-specific weights.
These weights enter the ultimate 𝜸 estimator and normal-theory standard errors.
Note that in the case of random-effect-as-outcome, the procedure reduces to the one described in Hanushek (1974).

text.text: These studies were followed by the random-effect-as-outcome case (Study 3).
We see two use-cases for this model structure.

First, one may wish to analyze the effect of multiple variables on a single random effect (rather than just a bivariate correlation), which a multiple-regression structural model is equipped to estimate.
Second, many linear MLMs with level-two predictors can be estimated under this framework (see Appendix B).

Thus, the random-effect-asoutcome case can be considered an approach to MLM estimation that reaps the benefits of other two-step procedures (e.g., isolating misspecification error) laid out in the introduction.
Finally, Study 4 combined the predictor and outcome cases by placing random effects on both sides of the structural equation.
The design represents two growth processes, each with its own MLM, in which the random intercept and slope of an earlier process predict the random slope of a later one.

text.text: Across studies, we hypothesized that naively using OLS with predictions would achieve minimal bias when the EB prediction (which we refer to as the "BLUP" for simplicity) is used as the predictor and the likelihood-only prediction is used as the outcome, following from Skrondal and Laake (2001).

text.text: However, minimal coefficient bias does not itself guarantee well-calibrated standard errors, coverage, or Type I error rates, particularly when precision varies across clusters or first-step parameters are estimated.
Thus, we investigated whether measurement error methods (e.g., M-MOM and 2S-PA) would improve both coefficient estimation and inference.

Additionally, in the case of heterogeneous cluster sizes (Study 2), we hypothesized that the measurement error methods would fare far better in terms of bias and other properties than simplified versions that do not account for heterogeneity (e.g., averaging measurement errors over people).
The divergence in performance would increase as heterogeneity became more severe.
In all cases, we posited that joint modeling would be the best benchmark for performance under adequate sample size, and would agree with the true target asymptotically.

Finally, we hypothesized that low-reliability conditions would lead to the largest advantage for methods that account for measurement error over those that do not and the worst cross-method performance.
As a corollary, we also expected large method differences for the dual process model (Study 4) when one process had low reliability while the other had high.

text.text: We evaluated estimator performance via five primary metrics.
First, we computed per-replication relative bias by dividing the raw bias by the true effect.
We report mean relative bias values as a percentage for interpretability.
Null conditions are excluded from relative bias summaries and instead inform Type I error.
Second, we computed the root mean square error (RMSE) of estimates across replications to investigate how well the estimator balances bias and variance simultaneously (James et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Second, we computed the root mean square error (RMSE) of estimates across replications to investigate how well the estimator balances bias and variance simultaneously <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(James et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Third, we investigated 95% coverage and standard error (SE) ratios (estimated SE divided by empirical SE) as measures of inferential performance.
The SE ratio is the mean reported standard error divided by the empirical standard deviation of the coefficient estimates from the same replications.
Fourth, we calculated Type I error rates in null (i.e. 𝛾 = 0) conditions.
Finally, we looked at convergence, defining converged replication as those producing a finite point estimate and a finite, positive standard error.
Model fitting programs often issue warnings in non-convergent cases.

Performance metrics are reported either on (a) the subset of replications for which all methods converged in step two ("shared") or (b) the subset of replications for which the method of interest converged in step two ("method-specific").
The former allows for comparisons across methods on identical datasets, while the latter allows for evaluation of each method's standalone performance conditional on convergence.
Metrics reported on scheme (b) also include convergence metrics for complete interpretation.
Coverage is conditional on convergence, rather than the probability of obtaining a covering interval across all attempted replications.

Random-effect predictions enable researchers to explore individual differences in within-person processes, yet treating these predictions as directly observed variables can bias estimates of relationships involving those processes and misrepresent their uncertainty.

In this work, we developed and evaluated Random-Effect Prediction Adjustment for Inference in Regression (REPAIR), a two-step method for estimating relationships among underlying person-specific processes and other variables.
REPAIR inverts the shrinkage in random-effect predictions to recover likelihoodonly predictions that represent the underlying random effects plus sampling error.
It then accounts for this error by incorporating person-specific sampling error covariances into a modified method-of-moments (M-MOM) structural regression.

Across four simulation studies, REPAIR generally recovered structural relationships well at medium to high predictor reliability, often had lower RMSE than alternative methods, and converged in every evaluated simulated dataset.
Our simulations illustrate why shrinkage and sampling error pose distinct challenges.

When a random slope was the structural outcome (Study 3), likelihood-only predictions removed the attenuation associated with using the BLUPs directly, and OLS regression yielded favorable estimates and standard errors in the conditions tested.

This result is consistent with additive outcome error contributing to residual variation without biasing coefficients when it is uncorrelated with the predictors (Skrondal & Laake, 2001); heterogeneous outcome precision may still require appropriate weighting or standard error adjustments to achieve accurate inference.

text.text: When random effects were predictors (Studies 1 and 2), however, removing shrinkage alone left substantial measurement-error-related attenuation.
Study 4 reinforced this conclusion: predictor-side reliability largely determined the difficulty of structural estimation when random effects appeared on both sides of the equation.
These findings also qualify the role-specific strategy of using BLUPs as predictors and likelihood-only predictions as outcomes (Skrondal & Laake, 2001).

text.text: In Study 4, this combination showed favorable median bias in some conditions, but low predictor reliability produced highly skewed estimates and extreme outliers.
A nearly unbiased median therefore did not establish stable estimation or accurate inference.
The implication is that the suitability of extracted predictions depends on their structural role and precision.

REPAIR provides a common additive-error representation and an explicit correction for those properties that addresses measurement error when random effects serve as predictors, outcomes, or both in a structural regression.
Across studies, predictor-side reliability was the most consistent determinant of REPAIR's performance.

With random-effect predictors (Studies 1 and 2), medium to high reliability generally yielded small bias, although small samples and correlated random intercepts and slopes remained challenging; at low reliability, bias was larger but generally decreased with sample size.
When a random slope served only as the outcome (Study 3), REPAIR showed minimal bias at every reliability level on its method-specific convergence subset.
With random effects on both sides of the equation (Study 4), high predictor reliability supported small bias regardless of outcome reliability.
Inferential performance generally followed a similar pattern.

Medium to high predictor reliability usually supported well-calibrated standard errors and approximately nominal confidence-interval coverage, whereas low reliability produced less consistent results, particularly in small samples.
However, coverage and Type I error did not always deteriorate together.
In Study 1 (predictor, homogeneous cluster sizes), for example, REPAIR's undercoverage for nonzero effects coexisted with conservative null rejection rates at low reliability.
This distinction matters because intervals centered on biased estimates can miss the true effect even when standard errors are not underestimated.
Study 2 (predictor, heterogeneous cluster sizes) further showed that preserving differences in precision helped REPAIR accommodate unequal observation counts.
With person-specific sampling error covariances, bias and coverage were generally less sensitive to cluster size heterogeneity than with the average measurement variants.
Those variants became increasingly attenuated as heterogeneity increased: under severe heterogeneity and low or medium reliability, their coverage fell below 80% at a sample size of 300.
Increasing sample size did not compensate for the averaging approximation in these conditions.
These findings support retaining person-specific shrinkage information when observation counts differ, consistent with Lai and Liu (2026).

Person-specific correction also did not eliminate all difficulties under low reliability and small samples but did mitigate the deterioration associated with heterogeneous observation counts.
When the structural relationship could be represented by a conventional cross-level interaction, REPAIR performed comparably to direct MLM estimation.
In Study 3 (outcome), both approaches achieved complete convergence, yielded minimal bias on their method-specific convergence subsets, and showed comparable standard errors, coverage, and RMSE.
REPAIR also compared favorably with MSEM, a joint-model benchmark for relationships involving latent random effects.
In several low-and medium-reliability settings, REPAIR produced less variable estimates and lower RMSE, despite MSEM sometimes showing smaller absolute bias.
These findings demonstrate that a regularized two-step method can offer favorable finite-sample performance relative to a correctly specified joint model.
Both REPAIR and 2S-PA offer two-step approaches that account for shrinkage and person-specific measurement error.

Whereas 2S-PA represents EB predictions as indicators of latent random effects and estimates their structural relationships through iterative likelihood estimation, REPAIR transforms the predictions to an additive-error scale and uses regularized moment calculations to estimate the structural regression.
This difference translated into substantial advantages for REPAIR in difficult conditions.
For example, in the low-reliability conditions of Study 1 (predictor, homogeneous cluster sizes), REPAIR achieved 100% convergence compared with 65.5% for 2S-PA.
Moreover, even on shared convergence subsets, REPAIR often had lower RMSE.
REPAIR therefore offers an alternative that combines the flexibility of two-step estimation with favorable numerical stability and estimation accuracy.
These advantages nevertheless require qualification when predictor reliability is low and samples are small.
REPAIR's greatest difficulties with bias and confidence interval coverage generally occurred in the same conditions that caused the most convergence failures among competing methods.
Although REPAIR continued to produce estimates, they could remain biased and their confidence intervals could miss the true effect more frequently than desired.
These problems generally diminished as sample size increased, although larger samples did not ensure nominal coverage in every condition.
Thus, REPAIR's numerical stability and frequently lower RMSE are useful advantages, but neither alone establishes that its confidence intervals are well calibrated.

REPAIR is a useful option when researchers wish to estimate structural relationships using predictions from separately fitted multilevel models, or to examine several structural models while holding the level 1 models fixed.
The latter is a motivation shared with other two-step latent-variable methods (Levy, 2023; Rosseel & Loh, 2024).

text.text: A direct MLM or other joint model remains an attractive option when it readily represents the scientific question.
The choice should therefore reflect how readily each approach accommodates the intended MLM and structural model.

For any structural model involving random effects, whether joint or two-step, we recommend checking the adequacy of the first-step MLM and the reliability of the individual effects (e.g., via the posterior reliability in Appendix A; see also Liu et al., 2021; Neubauer et al., 2020).

text.text: Our simulations offer initial planning benchmarks for REPAIR.

With randomeffect predictors, posterior slope reliabilities of .50 and .80 generally supported favorable performance, although small samples and correlated random effects remained challenging in some conditions.
At a reliability of .25, analyses with 30-50 clusters were particularly vulnerable to bias and poor coverage, and performance improved with more clusters.
In Study 4, for example, REPAIR generally showed minimal bias with 100 or more clusters, though this depended on reliability and effect size and is not a universal threshold.
Researchers should use these benchmarks to select candidate designs and then evaluate expected bias, coverage, and power through simulations tailored to their analysis.
The number of observations needed within each person depends on how much information those observations provide about the effects used as predictors.
Our simulations varied cluster size and calibrated reliability separately, so they do not identify a universal minimum number of repeated observations.
Researchers should instead assess whether their planned design is likely to yield adequately reliable effects.
When predictor reliability is low, collecting more observations per person or increasing the informative variation in the within-person predictor may improve precision.

For example, with the same number of observations, a person's linear rate of change can be estimated more precisely when assessments span the period of interest than when they are concentrated near a single time point.

We have also developed the repair R package, which fits step 1 models with common R backends (e.g., lme4; et al., 2015) and step 2 models with our M-MOM implementation, using standard formula syntax and C++ for computation.

Several questions remain for future research.
Our simulations evaluated correctly specified Gaussian MLMs and linear structural regressions.
Although robustness to misspecification is an important motivation for two-step methods (Bollen et al., 2007; Robitzsch, 2022; Rosseel & Loh, 2024), our studies did not examine this.

text.text: Future work should test misspecified mean and covariance structures, informative observation patterns, and departures from distributional assumptions.
We also focused on MLMs having homoskedastic, uncorrelated level 1 residuals.

The REPAIR equations already accommodate more general residual covariance structures through 𝑹 𝑗 , which enters both the likelihood-only prediction and its sampling-error covariance (Equations 4.6 and 4.7).
Evaluating performance with heteroskedastic or serially correlated residuals would therefore be a natural extension supporting longitudinal applications.
The choice of regularization for the second-step moment matrices warrants further study.
Our M-MOM implementation used the regularization proposed by Fuller (1987) with the minimum constant, 𝑝 + 1, keeping the correction close to its unregularized form.

The variants generally performed similarly, with selected improvements for the step-up variant, including bias in some Study 1 conditions.
Alternative choices proposed (e.g., Bogaert et al., 2023; Wall & Amemiya, 2000) could be evaluated for their effects on bias, RMSE, and confidence-interval coverage.

Related two-step methods account for first-step estimation uncertainty through corrected standard errors (e.g., Bogaert et al., 2023; Wall & Amemiya, 2000).

text.text: Future research should examine when these adjustments materially improve inference using REPAIR.
Finally, REPAIR's prediction-level correction requires each within-person random-effects design to have full column rank.
This is a limitation relative to joint models that can combine partial individual information when the overall model remains identified.
It is distinct from a singular estimated random-effect covariance, which does not prevent direct likelihood-only calculation.

Future extensions could retain estimable combinations of effects from incomplete individual records and recover structural moments by combining information across people (e.g., Botosaru & Powell, 2026).

text.text: REPAIR provides a two-step framework for structural regression with random effects as predictors, outcomes, or both.

Separating multilevel models from structural estimation allows researchers to retain models suited to their clustered data and use the resulting predictions to address relationships among underlying person-or cluster-specific effects and other variables.
This flexibility may be particularly useful for understanding relationships among person-specific processes that are measured across different tasks, settings, or timescales.
REPAIR enables researchers to use random-effect predictions in structural regression while explicitly accounting for their shrinkage and sampling error.

text.text: If one is interested in the population-level effect 𝛾 01 , standard joint estimation substitutes the level-two equations into the level-one equation and fits the resulting model.
However, the two-step approach estimates the individual equations one at a time, carrying uncertainty from the level-one equation to the leveltwo equation.
More specifically, the cluster-specific intercepts and slopes can first be estimated by GLS and then used as outcomes in the level-two equations.
The second step accounts for both their sampling-error covariances and the residual between-cluster variation represented by 𝑢 0 𝑗 and 𝑢 1 𝑗.
This retains the separate interpretation of the level-one and level-two equations while accounting for uncertainty in the estimated cluster coefficients.
This approach potentially reduces the effects of misspecification error (see Introduction) and is often more theoretically intuitive given how MLMs are typically formulated in psychology.
Additional study is required to assess the performance and generalizability of this framework.
We note that this representation requires full-column-rank cluster designs.
Moreover, when first-step covariance parameters are estimated, their samplingerror covariances enter as plug-in quantities.
Our work does not establish equivalence in efficiency to joint estimation or guarantee protection against model misspecification.
